articles.title: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102
articles.summary: Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life. Eva Marie Saint – a life in pictures. Her best films – ranked.
body: Eva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s, has died aged 102. Her screen work spanned six decades: Saint made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, starred in Alfred Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest, and in one of her last screen appearances played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film Superman Returns.
A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.

Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine which started with the prophetic words: “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – it followed her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful.
points: Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life.

body: “We’re investing in our future growth engines alongside our core ambitions in TV, Film and direct-to-consumer: Games, Experiences, Consumer Products, and Publishing,” Gordon wrote. “These are core pillars of our strategy to build engagement and fandom in both the physical and digital worlds. We want to meet consumers where they watch, play, and engage. body: Eddie Redmayne ‘s upcoming collaboration with Kore-eda Hirokazu is still at the screenplay stage, the Japanese filmmaker said Wednesday at a Busan International Film Festival press conference for his manga adaptation “Look Back.”

The festival has kept inviting Kore-eda back since his debut, and the opening ceremony even featured a piece of music named after him. “It is a city and a film festival for which I have exceptionally strong feelings,” he said.
He was joined by “Look Back” cast members Deguchi Natsuki, Makita Aju, Mori Nana and Ishikawa Ruka.

Kore-eda stumbled on the manga in a bookshop rather than through its serial run. “When I read it, I felt a shock like an impact,” he said. “It explored why people write stories, or in my case, why one makes films – that sort of creative impulse, or the heavy burden or karma that artists carry.”

articles.title: Skeet Ulrich Says His ‘Scream’ Arc Couldn’t Be Completed After Melissa Barrera’s Firing: ‘There’s No Billy Loomis’ Without Her
articles.summary: Skeet Ulrich, who starred in 1996’s “Scream” as Billy Loomis and later reprised the role in both 2022’s “Scream” and 2023’s “Scream VI,” has opened up about not being able to complete what he calls his “three-film arc” after his co-star, Melissa Barrera, was fired from the franchise.
body: After the firing, Barrera’s on-screen sister, Jenna Ortega, announced she wouldn’t return for 2026’s “Scream 7.” Neither Barrera nor Ulrich appeared in the recent film, which starred Matthew Lillard, Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, Isabel May, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Mason Gooding and others.
Last month, Lillard, who starred alongside Ulrich in the original film, admitted he felt “ashamed” for acting in “Scream 7” after Barrera was ousted.

“I went back to do ‘Scream,’ and I got called out. And I’m like, ‘Oh, fuck. That’s brutal,’” he said during a 30th anniversary screening of the original “Scream.” “I feel bad about that. I feel ashamed about that. Because in that moment I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey. I didn’t say no. I’m embarrassed; that’s the truth… I blew that. I’m on the wrong side of history for that. I still like being in the movie [but] it may not have been the best idea.”

articles.title: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire
articles.summary: New York film festival: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield. On the day that Luca Guadagnino ’s film about Sam Altman and OpenAI premiered, Vanity Fair released a cover story on Altman.
body: How much worse can things get? AI agents have already gone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases. Last year, a young woman used ChatGPT as a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.

Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studios pulled out of distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.

articles.title: ‘I’m bringing together women who nourish me’: French film-maker Alice Diop on her debut installation
articles.summary: The Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in Paris. Alice Diop has just returned to France from California when we speak.
body: Diop had been attending a two-week celebration of her work organised by the French department at University of California, Berkeley, in which academics pored over her documentaries ( Nous (We), Vers La Tendresse (Towards Tenderness)) and her first feature film, Saint Omer, which received the Silver Lion in Venice in 2022. The courtroom drama was inspired by a real trial that Diop attended, of a Senegalese woman who had allowed her baby to drown in the sea. Over two hours, it explored the complexities of race, culture and motherhood in contemporary France. The film was the first by a black female director to be entered by France as its official entry in the 2023 Academy Awards.

“To be studied like that, in such a temple of intellectual resistance, I was bowled over,” says Diop of UC Berkeley. “As a film-maker, it’s not up to me to analyse my work. But listening to them, it was good to feel understood.”

articles.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
articles.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.

The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.
It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.
The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.

articles.title: Apple and Dolby Bringing Dolby Atmos to Live Formula 1 Coverage
articles.summary: The audio company will deliver the roar of the engine and the mayhem of the pit lane to Apple TV viewers, beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix.
body: Apple wants Formula 1 fans to hear the roar of the engines, the squeals of the tires and the chaos of the pit lane as they’ve never heard it before.

The tech giant is partnering with Dolby Laboratories to bring its Dolby Atmos sound to F1, beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, later this month. The companies are betting that Atmos sound, paired with Dolby Vision, will make the races more exciting and visceral than they have ever been for viewers at home.

Apple, of course, is not a sports juggernaut like ESPN, nor is it pouring the same resources that, say, an Amazon Prime Video is putting into the space. Instead, the tech company has decided that whatever sports it does invest in, it wants to create the best experience possible for viewers, including video nd sound quality that is a step above what is available elsewhere.

articles.title: Jack White Slams Trump for Saying Iran Can “Take Out” L.A. and San Diego: “The Worst American of All Time”
articles.summary: "A U.S. 'President' that recommended that two major cities in our country be bombed because they don't give total allegiance to his ego. Imagine any other President or elected official in history saying this," the musician wrote.
body: Jack White is once again slamming Donald Trump, this time over the president’s comments suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it were allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.

On Monday, Trump was speaking at a campaign rally in Nebraska, where he defended the war in Iran despite Americans’ concerns about the economic impact. The president called it a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe” and “keeping our country safe.”

Trump suggested that Iran could “take out” an American city if the country was to develop a nuclear weapon. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” he added, as the crowd cheered.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom also denounced Trump’s remarks, calling the president “deranged and dangerous.” He added in another post on X, “An American president is talking about Los Angeles and San Diego being ‘taken out.’ Where the hell is Congress? This is dangerous. The time to stand up is NOW.”

articles.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
articles.summary: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?
body: It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
